utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I understand that it was snowing outside, so the traffic may be very difficult at this moment. So shall we start? Ms. Chana, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Chana: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jasarevic. Before the break yesterday, we were discussing this document, MFI215, which was this report on the matters in Grabovica and it was addressed to you personally. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever have occasion to meet Mr. Dzankovic personally over this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From late 1993, I don't think that I've ever seen Dzankovic since then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the matter of this -- the crimes which had been committed in the village of Grabovica. You got the report. You gave various taskings. Was it just in -- in a written communication or did you ever meet with him personally?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he left the security administration in late 1993. If I remember correctly, it's either late 1993 or early 1994. Sometime in that period. He left the security administration. He was working somewhere else. So I didn't really have the opportunity to see him again and talk to him about this matter, except for the period when he was at the administration following his return from Grabovica. That is understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you talk to him about the crimes committed in Grabovica, face to face?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the discussion? What was the nature of this discussion when you met him?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I wasn't his immediate superior. Mr. Dzankovic had two other officers between him and myself. He had the chief of the sector and then chief of the department and then me. At the beginning, Dzankovic seemed a little bit resigned, a bit frightened, dissatisfied. Of course, as far as I can remember that now, I was not satisfied with his reactions. It seemed to me as if he were disorganised, worked in a disorganised manner. I wasn't satisfied with the way he was coping. Perhaps I was expecting a bit more. At the time and now, I objectively felt that he couldn't give more, work better. I don't know whether there were any other reasons for that, but he was a bit discouraged and perhaps those things contributed to his leaving the military security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I'm asking about the discussions which took place between you and Dzankovic when you met over this issue about the crimes committed in Grabovica. Can you please assist the Court and tell them what were the nature of these discussions? What did you say to each other, in respect of this one matter and this one meeting, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In spite of my best efforts, I really cannot recall such particulars. This was a long time ago, and my thinking right now about the way he worked then is more based on reports rather than conversations we had at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever report back to you about his ability to investigate this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he did. I cannot remember that either. If he did submit a report of any kind, that would be recorded somewhere. But I did receive his report from the field dated the 10th of October in response to the tasks that I set out for him when he left on the 21st of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself follow up this matter in any other way?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what time period and what matter?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The crimes in Grabovica. You gave some taskings to various people, as I recall, in your testimony yesterday and you also put forward this information to the six addressees. Is there anything else you yourself did in this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the question now. Yes. When I talked about the drafting of the plan to resolve the problem of lack of discipline in the 1st Corps with the glaring examples of the 9th and 10th Brigades in this respect, the event in Grabovica, the crime there only speeded up the implementation of that commitment to resolve that problem the way this happened. Before that, all the information and the reports that we received from the field were included in other reports which were then sent to all the addressees that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in respect of these particular crimes which you got notice of from various sources, did you yourself do anything else?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than what I've already said, including them into reports which were forwarded to our superiors, the security service of the 1st Corps was informed about this and then teamwork followed, organised in the Trebevic operation, according to a special plan and in which I participated in team number 2, the team for operational evaluation of that problem -- the task -- and also reviewing the tasks of the problem for Trebevic I and Trebevic II, which followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was an IKM in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that there was an IKM in Jablanica. I already commented on that in my earlier testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware around 24th September 1993 that the same troops who had been accused of committing these crimes in the village of Grabovica were to be redeployed in another military operation? Were you aware of any information of that nature?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would now like to show you a document, Mr. Jasarevic, and that's MFI217, Your Honours. It's 04036168.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry, it's 6182.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I -- I apologise for interrupting. I -- I seem to have the B/C/S version of that on my screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just clarify this particular document. It's 167, 65 ter number, and it's 04036168.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'm now ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me about this document, Mr. Jasarevic. Can you please tell me who is it from and who is it to and whether you've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen this document before obviously, because up here there is a remark of mine about these two tasks. Again, it's addressed to Vahid Bogunic. And then it says that he should be informed about it, as my deputy. He's a person who deals with counter-intelligence affairs. The second task is Dzevad Jusic. He was the superior officer in the security administration, and he carried out the counter-intelligence protection of the Supreme Command Staff, so it was given to him to review all the options of using the Rotor source. Yesterday I spoke a lot about operational or operative work, different aspects of that. So this document was drafted as a product of operative work. The source refers to Rotor. He provided information from the security service of the 1st Corps and this information was relayed to me via this document. Obviously this document was something that was in my possession and I had indicated all the tasks on the document, as you can see up at the top of the paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to page 2 in the English. I don't know what -- I think it's probably the same page for you. You've only got one page. It's about the fourth paragraph. And it's -- and it starts "At the meeting ...." Are you with me, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, "At the meeting, Halilovic requested that the units or parts of units under the command of the above-stated persons be prepared and sent towards the Herzegovinian theatre of war, which they refused." Rotor then states that around 0200 hours can the Halilovic phoned Delalic and requested him to carry out his own. Delalic's order is not known to Rotor." Mr. Jasarevic, does that mean that these troops were to be redeployed for another military operation? Was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot interpret this in any more detail than it's stated here. The only thing I can do is to assume that this should have been to some extent a continuation of the combat that was going on in the Herzegovina area, most probably, in September, in early September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the troops were to continue the combat operations - is that right - in early September?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has scrupulously continued to indicate that this is just operative information. He's not to be asked to comment upon it as if it's true by my learned friend. If he had an opinion, if he knew about combat operations in Herzegovina, then my friend can certainly ask him about that. But the objection is to the question as it's currently framed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Chana, first of all, you have to ask a question whether this witness knew about that operation or not or knew about this document or not and to lay the proper foundations for your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think the witness has indicated that he had actually marked on the document and he had seen it. And my question was not as much, Your Honours, on the truth of the -- of the matter but the fact that that's what the document reflects, and I think that's what the witness has already said. So I'll move on from that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, now I would like to ask you about Trebevic -- Operation Trebevic, that you talked about earlier, and you were going to tell the Chamber before I interrupted you yesterday about the various teams which were deployed in this operation. Can you please now detail for the Chamber about these teams and what Trebevic operation was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Trebevic operation, in accordance with the decision of the Presidency and the Supreme Command, was implemented by the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the MUP. The objective of the operation was to deal with deviant conduct and those units which were outside of the regular command and control system, primarily the parts of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; namely, the 9th and the 10th Brigades of that corps. The reason the Trebevic operation was speeded up was because of the crime in Glogovac [as interpreted]. There was a plan already for the implementation of this operation, and yesterday I already said that it was especially grave and difficult task that everyone was facing in order to make sure that the defence of the city of Sarajevo remained intact and that it shouldn't be jeopardised in any way. The plan was sets up in such a way that it was implemented through teams. That's what we called them conditionally, which were those who were supposed to carry out this plan. There were three teams. The first team was the command and control team of the operation, comprising the commander of the army, Mr. Rasim Delic; the MUP minister, Mr. Bakir Alispahic; the commander of the 1st Corps, Mr. Vahid Karavelic. That was number-one control and command body. Team number 2 was in charge of operative work for the compilation of operative data and all those tasks which are part of that particular professional skill. I was in that team on behalf of the army security service administration. Mr. Nedzad Ugljen was also a part of the team. And as an assassination attempt was made against him, and it succeeded, so the person is unfortunately no longer alive. Also the deputy minister for defence was also one of his posts. The third person in this team was Mr. Sacir Arnautovic, who was the chief of the military security service. The third team with the team for the immediate control of the units -- direct control of the units, which according to the plan and the evaluation were to take part in the blockade of the command of the units which were the subjects of the operation and the ones that were creating a problem. That was one of the most serious aspects of this operation, how to actually deal with that particular matter to avoid a large number of casualties. We did expect casualties. We made very precise estimates, made a valuation of all the options. The third team included the deputy commander of the 1st Corps, Mr. Ismet Dahic; the commander of the special MUP unit, Mr. Dragan Vikic; and the commander of the military police of the General Staff, Mr. Dzevad Radzo [phoen]. These were the three teams that were leading the operation, and in the control and command aspect implemented the Trebevic I operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can -- can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, just -- may I just intervene there. There was a reference there to -- at page 8, line 8 to what's being translated as the village of Glogovac. My instructions are that -- that it sounded as if it was Grabovica and it might be important for the witness just to clarify whether there's a translation error or whether that's what he meant. I'm -- because for myself, I can't hear. So -- I'm sorry to interrupt my friend, and it's not a criticism. It's just that that issue arose and I think that perhaps is now to time to fix it, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Yes, it was Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see yes, the -- the record reveals that the interpreter has corrected that to Grabovica, and I'm satisfied with that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jasarevic. Would you tell us then about this operation and how -- whether it was implemented -- implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than the teams that I mentioned, significant forces were also planned to be used in a blockade if there was a conflict with these people. The leadership was very decisive in its intention to deal with this problem. If I remember well, seven or eight units were allocated and they were standing by just in case they were needed. This was a tactical aspect. They were to operate in two levels. First were the special units of the MUP and the army. They went directly to the command posts of these brigades. Some units were blocked where they were in order to prevent any unforeseen reactions and so that these units could be stopped. The second layer or level was planned in a way that units were taken from other brigades about the strength of a battalion, because it was impossible to predict exactly what would happen. So these units were planned to be used in the second echelon just in case they were needed. The very beginning of the operation was prepared and conducted in the greatest of secrecy. All of us who were taking part in that operation, from the Presidency down, were concerned that if the units found out about this, the units against whom the operation was directed, there could be some incidents. It was especially important to us to avoid any units leaving the lines. On the other hand, it was very important to keep such information confidential because of the enemy forces, because purely from a military point of view if the enemy found out that we were dealing with such serious problems within our own ranks, in our own house, so to speak, it would be favourable for them to launch an offensive against us, and then they would be in a favourable position. That is why secrecy was an extremely important factor in the operation. Perhaps I could be wrong in some details, but I think that around 1.00 a.m. on the 25th, 26th October the president made this decision. He actually launched the operation or gave the word that the operation should be launched. At about 2.00 a.m., we found ourselves at the MUP building, and we acted in accordance with the elements that I mentioned. The units from the first echelon that I mentioned had developed their own part of the tasks. Each one of the teams did that. These units had such positions which enabled them to quickly block the commands of the units. We had estimated that not all the units were of the same opinion as their extremist members were, but some of these extremist members of the units were able to maybe carry the rest of the -- the troops along with them. So that was one of our concerns. This task was carried out quite successfully in the 9th Brigade. We had very good operative positions there. This would prove to be a very good thing later. And this enabled us to very easily convince Ramiz Delalic to surrender himself. He agreed to talk and then surrendered, so there was no clash in that particular instance, and he was detained. There were some other people, and this will turn out to be so later, because we're talking about several hundred people who were detained that night and the next day to the physical culture hall in the centre of Sarajevo; that's where they were taken. There was a major problem concerning the 10th Brigade, however. I don't know whether some tactical mistakes were made there, as that unit and their command was being approached. I don't know. I'm not able to give any comments on that particular aspect of the operation. But what happened there was that Caco and his closest security and inner command put up resistance. While putting up armed resistance, they practically massacred three men from the military police crimes platoon of the General Staff, which included the son of a very respectable man, an official in the MUP and then later in the army. We're talking about Hebib, the son of Mr. Avdo Hebib. Some details were talked about later. I think they also turned up in reports, stating that they had thrown him from I don't know which floor down to the concrete. They also stabbed him with knives, shot him with pistols. I can't remember all the details. They're perhaps not all that important. But anyway, a battle erupted, and Caco, who would be killed later, that morning and that afternoon on the 26th, the command post of the 10th Brigade, the conflict there resulted in 15 or 16 people being killed. Perhaps I'm wrong by one or two numbers. We could see that things were becoming very complicated there and would not be resolved so easily. The state leadership was very concerned. This was not only the problem of an individual but it was a problem that caused concern to the entire military, political, and police leadership. We were trying to find a way to approach Caco, to get him to surrender in order to prevent even greater casualties, to prevent his own men from getting killed. All the time there was the fear that if this was something that the enemy on the hills found out about, then they would use that and that would really create chaos and they would try to enter the town. I know that several people made an attempt and finally Mr. Jusuf Pusonja, if I remember correctly, succeeded in getting in touch with Caco, Musan Topalovic, Caco, and his inner circle of security, and they managed to convince him to give himself up and they took him to the 1st Corps. He was given assurances that he would not be abused, that he would be given a fair trial, and so on and so forth. So he and that group of people who were immediately around him were taken to the 1st Corps. So after the very first initial triage, he was taken to the central prison with that group. That's where they were all detained. They were taken into custody. There's a police report about this. Because there was no electricity in Sarajevo at that time. It was dark. It was already night, very late in the day on the 26th of October. According to the police reports at the time there was Kralja Tomislava Street which runs into Titova Street. He tried to escape in a van that had two back doors. This was stated in the police report because the park was very close to the sidewalk. It was about 1 to 1.5 metres away from the sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. These are details which are very interesting but perhaps not so helpful to Their Honours. Now, you said that the plan was successful --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, my friend did ask the question, and it's a little unfair to cut it off at that vert moment. The next detail may have some relevance and it should be allowed to finish. I think the witness was probably one line away from finishing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if there's only one line left, so let the witness finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What were you going to say, Mr. Jasarevic. Finish your one line, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A line or two maybe. Caco tried to escape. He tried to escape to the nearby park. The police officers who were escorting him opened fire and at daybreak the next day he was found in the park. He had been killed or seriously wounded. I can't remember exactly what the police found. But what was ascertained is that he was killed while trying to escape, while he was being escorted. That's all I have to say about that, but I can tell you about the triage at the FIS building with several hundred people involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not quite -- I don't understand the word "triage." What's the meaning of the word "triage"?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the action, lots of people were detained, whoever was within the command area, people belonging to the brigade. This was done because of the lack of trust, because not all the details could be foreseen. I think hundreds of people were detained, maybe 500 or 600 people, although I may be wrong about the figure, and more than 50 operations officers whose assistance was enlisted by the MUP, the 1st Corps, the State Security Service, were detached from their brigades. People from four or five different bodies, 50 or 60 operatives, who briefly screened the people assembled there. Those who had been picked up, they checked to see who should remain there and who should be released. They wanted to see which of those people rounded up had committed violations of discipline. Several hundred statements were taken after detention was determined, several hundred statements. Four copies were made of each: One to the military prosecutor, one to the MUP, and one to the administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Sefer Halilovic during this time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, during this time there was no trust in Sefer Halilovic. As far as I remember, the reason was to keep the brigades from learning about the operation. This was based on operative information which, if memory serves, we spoke about in great detail yesterday. Mr. Halilovic was in his office with his security people. I think it was the next day or perhaps two days later. I was given an assignment by these teams running the operation to get in touch with Mr. Sefer Halilovic and tell him that he should be interviewed in the State Security Service. I went to see him and told him that he should come with me to the MUP building. His driver, Mr. Halilovic, and I all got into the car and we set out. I noticed that Mr. Sefer Halilovic was visibly excited. I'm not sure if I should say "frightened." But it was clearly visible that he was in an unpleasant position. He was not being arrested, as I told him. He was just coming for an interview. He asked me, "Jusuf, am I under arrest," something along these lines. I can't remember the specific wording. And I said, "Chief, sir, you are not under arrest. You are just going for an interview." His response was very soldierly and very disciplined. I took him to the MUP building. He was interviewed by two individuals. I know their names, but I don't know what happened later on. One of them was Borisa Delic, an experienced state security officer. Before the war, he used to be chief of the Sarajevo State Security Service. And the other man was from the security administration. He was chief of one of the sectors in the counter-intelligence department. He had no rank at the time, but he was soon to be promoted to the rank of colonel, Hamzo Popovic. Even before the war, he was a security officer. He had been trained to work as a security officer. They had a lot of respect for Mr. Halilovic and his authority, so two very experienced officers were selected from the security service to conduct this interview. I was not present during the interview, nor did I ever drive Sefer Halilovic there again or drive him back. He was treated fairly. I have never heard anything to suggest otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Sefer Halilovic after this, this time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interview went on for several days. Throughout the operation, one was in permanent communication with Mr. Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency. One used a messenger because one tended not to trust phone calls. I can't specify the time intervals, but they would often get in touch with the president to ask his opinion and position. They would also report to the president. As concerns Mr. Sefer Halilovic, as far as I remember, because I never talked to the president myself, although I talked to the gentlemen who were part of the teams, especially the team of which I was a member, and these persons told me that the president was adamant that Sefer should be treated in a fair manner. He greatly appreciated Sefer's contribution to the army, how the army was developed and what his contribution was as a professional officer. Eventually when a criminal report was filed against Sefer Halilovic, which I didn't actually see but I was told that one had been filed -- according to my information, although I didn't hear this directly - this is just a piece of information that I had at the time - this criminal report was stopped and Mr. Halilovic was not prosecuted. There were no further attempts to prove him guilty following that report. As is well known - I'm not sure about the specific date, whether it was right after or a little later - Mr. Halilovic was retired, prior to which he had been promoted to the rank of general. I thought this was some sort of a sop but also a sort of recognition that he received for his work and his contribution. It is important to point out, Your Honours, that throughout the operation the military prosecutor was being updated permanently on what was going on. There was constant ongoing cooperation. This cooperation was very lively, both day and night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. I just want to show you a couple of more documents before I complete your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown MFI157 -- sorry, 65 ter number 157, which is MFI218. And it's 04036182.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see this document, Mr. Jasarevic? Could you please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen this document before, but what I see here certainly helps to jog my memory. I am here giving an assignment to Vahid Bogunic to provide assignments and instructions to the sector for the counter-intelligence protection of the Main Staff and command. What you see here in bold letters, "A/A," and then the initials here, this was the chief of the section, Mr. Dzevad Jusic and here you see my signature. The analytical department had the task to unite information from documents by the 1st Corps. Was it before or later? This is 17/64 and this is 17/63. So this is a document by the 1st Corps security, and this was done, but on page 2 I see the stamp, and this is the 2nd or the 12th -- about the 2nd of March, 1994; whereas, on this document, the date I see is the 8th of October. I'm not sure how this discrepancy in date came about. Oh, by the way, I'm not sure if I've said this before: Throughout 1994, the military security service was within the administration of the Defence ministry. It was no longer attached to the Main Staff. I have seen this document before, and this is what it speaks about. It speaks about information --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I just intervene for a moment there. I have a problem on my screen here. It may be that this document is similar to or the same as the previous document, but it looks to me as if I've got the same document on the screen as I had before. And I -- perhaps I could think just confirm that it's -- it's not an administrative error; in fact, what is being done here is that my friend is tendering another copy of the same document that may have different markings on it or -- I'm just not quite sure what I am looking at now, frankly, I'm sorry to say. So could that just be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Let me confirm. The document the witness is looking at. This is dated 7th October 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct? And it has an attachment to it. Is that correct, Mr. Jasarevic? I don't know whether learned counsel has got the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, sorry, yes, I can confirm -- I think I have got that same document, at least the front page of it, as the Court may have, dated the 7th, but when my friend refers to an attachment, at the moment I only have the first page up in front of me, so I can't confirm that. And I think the witness is referring to some notations upon it in the B/C/S version, and we have the English version, so we -- we don't -- we can't see that. It's just that a previous exhibit appeared to be this document some -- some, say, ten minutes ago, and I don't know whether this is another copy of the same document or whether it's one which was written on subsequently. And I think that just should be confirmed just so that we know which one we're dealing with, for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I correct the record and state the numbers again. This is -- was 65 ter, was 157. Now it's MFI217, and the number is 04036182. It may look similar to the old document, but this is certainly a new document, and it's got 10-page addition to it. Your Honour, perhaps that's the problem with e-court. You can't see the entire document at one time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the attachment, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the attachment, but there's something I don't understand. Page 1 of this document is dated the 7th of October, 1993. What I saw at the time or what I suggested with my handwriting on the upper right-hand side and the attachments I have bear the dates 2nd of March, 1994. And this is what confuses me. And I can't see -- when I look at these attachments, it's impossible for me to conclude who they belong to because I didn't normally leave a document unsigned. That is why I was confused by these attachments. Page 1 is all right. There is nothing strange about page 1. But I find the attachments very confusing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if I show you another document. I'll leave this document, Mr. Jasarevic. And which is 04036297, MFI218.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just enquire what's the 65 ter number of that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The 65 ter number is 158.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't bear my initials or the instructions that I would usually include. Based on that, I would include that I have not seen this document before. However, I commented on a very similar document yesterday. This was produced by the State Security Service, and it shows a cross-section of their operative information, the information that they forwarded. What I said about yesterday's document is what I can say about this one. This is operative information, the sort of information that we used, since this is a highly respected institution, the institution that produced this document. We used this information to produce our special reports and our reports to our superiors. I explained that this is a document containing operative information. And if I may also add, that this document was not signed or stamped and it wasn't filed except by the security administration once it had arrived. It wasn't filed. I can't see the file number that should have been placed there by the state security. You can see the number of the copy and you can see that this document is a state secret. This was only possible with the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, because in the army we used the term "military secret." I'm not sure what else I should say in addition to the comments I made yesterday about operative information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the information is similar in both these --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Wait. Just a minute, please. Well, I object to this being taken any further. Given what the witness has now said, he doesn't say he's seen it. Again, the situation is if my friend has to -- has evidence that she wants to elicit from this witness as to matters relevant to Mr. Halilovic, well, of course that's legitimate. But we're now back in the same position. This is effectively not his document. He may know something about operative measures. In fact, he obviously does know something about operative measures. And in the times somewhere around the offences that Mr. Halilovic is charged with, that may be relevant. We've now moved into March 2000 -- sorry, March 1994, and the remoteness problem I mentioned earlier is very acute, in addition to the objection that this witness didn't see this document. So I object to any further questions based on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes. I think, first of all, the Prosecution has to establish the relevance of this document to this very case. Secondly, I -- it mate ask some questions to this witness concerning the contents of this document, whether he's familiar with the contents or not; although, we understand that the witness has never seen this document. It is not his document at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, is this document basically a report on Delalic and in some respects Halilovic, this operative information in this?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the document is indeed about these two persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose document was it and who was it to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite obviously this is a document by the State Security Service, and it was sent to the security administration, as I said yesterday, on account of the Trebevic I and Trebevic I operations, you see what they included in the heading is "Supreme Command Staff" and "security administration." There is no detail here to show, with the exception of the incoming stamp -- there is nothing to indicate that the security administration produced this document or obtained this information. We took this to be operative information and included it as such in our reports, signed and stamped, sent off to our superiors. I'm not sure if I make myself sufficiently clear, but I think I could go on repeating this same answer for ages now, because there's really nothing more specific that I can say, that I could really stand by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is the document that you produced, that is, the security administration? Is that what you just said, that it's the document that you yourself produced?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm trying to confirm from -- is that what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. No, by no means. No, I didn't produce this document. I never said that I produced this document. In that case, I would have signed it. You'd be able to see my file number. It wouldn't be a state security document. It would be a military secret document in that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about you yourself producing it. Did it come from the security administration?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It didn't come from the security administration. This document didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the information in this document similar to the information in the last document I showed you, in the attachment?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was produced in a similar way and used in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you'd give me a moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all I have from this witness in my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that we should have a break at this moment, and after that we'll have the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just raise one matter before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As indicated yesterday at the end of cross-examination the Prosecutor was going to indicate to this Tribunal whether or not the Prosecutor had in their possession tapes and transcripts upon which my friend justified the introduction of and use of a particular document. And I now seek that that answer be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Chana, are you in the position to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This particular transcript has been disclosed to the Defence. It's in our 65 ter list as 104. It's a conversation between Celo and another individual. This witness has basically said he does not know about this -- any -- any intercepts, so we will now produce this particular intercept through the relevant person, Your Honour, because that person is also on our witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you mean you have other witnesses to testify concerning of that document in the future?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The intercept, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The intercept. Yes, is this satisfactory, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. Yes and no, Your Honour. It's a satisfactory answer so that I know what the document is. It's not a very satisfactory basis for putting it to this witness. I thought the basis for putting it to this witness was that there was no one else. But I'm -- perhaps I misunderstood about that. But in any event, my friend has identified the tape and -- well, the transcript. And I take it that what's being referred to is a transcript which is currently listed as 104. That's been identified by my friend. That's the information I need. So I'm grateful for that to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, shall we take the break right now. And we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Morrissey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jasarevic. I just want to ask you a couple of questions about Trebevic, the operation, in a very general sense first of all. And first of all, could I ask you this: You mentioned in your evidence in chief that late? July - and I think you might have said the 28th of July - there was a meeting of the Council for the Protection of Constitutional Order at which you spoke. Now, first of all, have I got the date of that right? Was that the 28th of July?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot speak about the exact date because I don't remember it, but it was in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. Jasarevic, too you may feel free in regard to -- when I put a date to you that's too specific, you can always tell me that. In any event, at the end of July, at some stage late in July, there was a meeting of that council, at which you attended; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that meeting, you put certain proposals and made certain suggestions about which you spoke yesterday. Yes. And what -- what followed from that -- could I just ask you, was that -- from that time on you and those senior persons present at the meeting were all aware of the need to deal in a systematic way with the disciplinary failure of the leadership of the 9th and 10th Brigades; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you whether the name of Operation Trebevic was invented at that time or was that a later development?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a later development.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when the name "Trebevic" came to be attached to this general idea of dealing with the problems of the leadership of the 9th and 10th?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date, but I think this happened after Grabovica, possibly in late September, early October. That is when more immediate preparations began to implement that operation and the drafting of the plan for the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- so I have some questions about the earlier phase of -- of this operation, and I want to find a useful word because the word "operation" has got various connotations in this -- in this case. Would you be comfortable with me using the term "goal" in this context, by which I mean after that meeting, you and the senior leaders at the meeting shared a goal of dealing with the leadership problems of the 9th and 10th?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goal was primarily to bring those two brigades in line, in terms of carrying out the tasks of the 1st Corps. That was the basic goal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. And in particular, to bring them within a mature and predictable version of the system of command and control -- sorry, control and command, "rukovodjenje," and "komondovanje"; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there were a number of problems confronting you in your attempts to bring about this goal, and I want to go through some of those problems with you. First of all, it's the fact that the 9th Brigade was defending an important part of the front line in Sarajevo; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same can be said of the 10th Brigade in their area of -- of responsibility; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so that in dealing with the leadership problems of either of those brigades, you had to bear in mind the need not to compromise the -- the very defence of Sarajevo itself; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I suppose there might be said to be two aspects to that: First of all, generally speaking those brigades were populated by good soldier who is did their job very well; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the vast majority. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't want your operation to destroy the effectiveness of those fighting soldiers who were doing such a good job; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And secondly -- and this is -- I'm putting a proposition. Feel free to comment on it, however. The very way in which the matter was handled might have implications elsewhere in the army. For example, if you marched into Caco's headquarters and tried to arrest him, that might trigger discomfort and unhappiness in other sections of the army. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand -- and in truth, we now have the gift of hindsight with these matters, but at the time you could never be sure precisely what the effect of a particular initiative would be; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Nevertheless, from the time of that meeting of the Council of the Constitutional Order late in -- in July, you and other senior persons began to collect information designed to help you bring about the goal of returning the 9th and 10th to the system of control and command; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this information began to be collected in a more intensive way than initially thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm going to come to ask you some questions about the effect that the tragedies at Grabovica and Uzdol had on your -- on your goals in a few moments. I just have some questions about the time before that, before I get to that phase. Now, therefore, in the course of -- of collecting that information, I take it there was -- there were more organisations involved than your organisation, which is the SVB, or military security organisation; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps just to explain something to the Court here because we have many military bodies with initials connected to them. The SVB is the name for the military security service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you just explain to the Tribunal what the UB was and how that related to the SVB and what part of the SVB was the UB.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UB is an abbreviation for Uprava Besbjenosti [phoen], which was at the top of the military security service in the expert sense and it was located in the army's Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Was there -- and just -- you can assist the Court here -- the Tribunal here too with this: Moving aside from military security now into the normal civilian organs, and in particular the MUP, civilian police, did the civilian police also have a professional service attaching to it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the security -- state security. The "SDB" would be the abbreviation for it in documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And because we sometimes see the abbreviation SDB, when we see that, that is a -- an organ of the civilian police, as you've described. Does that have a similar top-level body such as the UB within it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is slightly different than the military organisation. The security service and the military organisation is an element, one of several elements within the organisation. The State Security Service within the MUP is a component which is conditionally speaking more powerful than the military security service within the military organisation, and it includes the intelligence or the offensive function as well as the counter-intelligence protective service, this in the police sense, and this is the characteristically crucial part of the Secret Service within the internal affairs service. That's within the State Security Service. The difference between the two services, when we're talking about the basic operational or work methods, but in spite of these differences in organisation their methods of work are more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I understand that. And now, in terms of -- of the goals that emerged from the Council for the Protection of Constitutional Order, I was asking you whether your organisation, the SVB, was the only organisation collecting information, and you said, "No, it wasn't." Now, is it the fact that the -- the MUP units, and in particular state security, was actively involved in collecting such information during this time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As it happens, this service was more highly developed and they managed to compile more valuable and greater amounts of information than the military security service did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it's -- it appears from some of the documents that you were asked to comment upon by the Prosecution in this matter that you would sometimes have forwarded to you as operative information material from the MUP. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that situation, you had the duty to note and to process and in an appropriate case to pass on that information in reports, regardless of whether or not it was reliable or unreliable but simply as operative information. Is that true and accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that sense, I made my comments earlier. In view of the seriousness of the service providing such information and in view of the fact that their work methodologies were even more powerful and stronger than ours, and in view of the circumstances in wartime, we did not usually do that nor did we feel the need to check such information that was acquired during our operative work. We also didn't feel any need to keep them to ourselves. We would process them and then pass them on along the proper lines to our superiors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And it would be -- I mean obviously I wasn't there, but you tell me the answer to this: You weren't required to behave like a military judge or a -- or even an investigating prosecutor in dealing with this information. In one sense, your business was information and you had to deal with this information, whatever its quality. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dealing with the information that we received didn't involve the same procedures that you would have in a court. There was no need to check them in the same way. This information was more used as an argument to evaluate the situation, to create - let me put it that way - some kind of responsible position or for the purposes of being cautious. And that is what this information was used for and that's how it was looked at. May I just add that the term that we used would be indicative information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And I appreciate that you have answered these questions to some degree already with the -- with the Prosecutor. But in the course of gathering that information, whether it was gathered by your organisation or by the state security organisations, this information, I take it, was shared around among those persons who were concerned -- among those people who had been at the Council for the Protection of Constitutional Order and who were directly concerned with the goal that you've mentioned; is that accurate? Council for --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Except not all those who used our information were members of the Council for the Protection of Constitutional Order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those who shared this information, I take it, were people trusted to help bring about the goals of -- the goals that you desired, effectively. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at that time, Sefer Halilovic, because of certain operational information you had, did not enjoy that same level of trust among those who were present at the Council for the Protection of Constitutional Order; is that a fair statement of reality?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that explicitly with a yes or a no. It was up to each person. It was their personal position on how they understood such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, sorry. And perhaps I -- I should have put the question more precisely. I'll put it another way, though: Halilovic himself was not invited to that meeting; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's the fact that some people - and I'm talking now about the representatives from the MUP, from the Ministry of the Interior side of things - expressed a concern that Halilovic -- Sefer Halilovic might not promote these goals that you're talking about. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer Halilovic in that period was not the number-one person in the army. It was Commander Rasim Delic. And that is the reason amongst other things why Delic attended that meeting. This second part of your question: Yes, for sure the operative information which we saw in certain documents implied a risk that the preparations for forthcoming activities could be leaked and could reach those people we did not want to find out about that, and that is why there was this kind of reserve regarding Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by "reserve," you don't mean anything sinister, but what I mean, I take it, by "reserve" is that the information gathered in pursuit of these goals was not shared with Sefer Halilovic. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the tragedies at Grabovica and -- and Uzdol ultimately came to the knowledge of your group - by the term "your group," I mean those who were at this council meeting - when the news of the tragedies came to your group, that provided a further and more urgent reason to press ahead with plans for decisive action concerning the commands of the 9th and 10th; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that accelerated the setting of the date for the start of this operation, probably accelerated it by maybe 15 to 20 days or something, but it did accelerate it. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to be frank, the news of these killings were a shock to everybody concerned because -- perhaps I'll deal with the matter more specifically. In terms of the 9th Brigade, you had information that they -- they were involved in the trench-digging activities, which you've testified about, and you also knew of some acts of individual criminality and dishonesty, about which you've -- well, I'm going to start this question again because it's becoming too general. You knew about certain improper and indeed criminal acts by the 9th Brigade before this time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that I knew about the criminal acts by the 9th Brigade. I knew about the lack of discipline there, but I never said anything about the criminal acts, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I really was referred to that issue with the jeep, and that's why I became specific. But frankly, you didn't foresee that the -- any soldiers from the 9th Brigade were going to go and massacre a whole village of innocent, old, and apparently friendly Croatian civilians; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, but I didn't know that that brigade would be there or that it happened to be in that village. Of course, I couldn't assume that that unit could do anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. All right. And just to jump forward a moment. You came to know because of the Pazaric incident on the 8th of September that elements of the 9th Brigade were indeed going to Herzegovina; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the report indicated that we had here, but it didn't immediately make me think about Neretva 93. I will actually find out the name of it later. These two things were not immediately connected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And frankly, Mr. Jasarevic, I'm not trying to connect them. What I'm really focussing on is that the 9th Brigade had some problems but it was a shock to you when you found out the allegations about what happened, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was shocked, absolutely, when I found out about the crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once the crime was -- came to your knowledge - and later I'm going to ask you some questions about the actions taken in the professional capacity by the H -- by the SVB, but these are still general questions - once that information came to your knowledge, the -- the people who had been at the Council for the Protection of Constitutional Order intensified their efforts to collect information about the 9th Brigade's activities, including these terrible events; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could respond with a "yes"; although, not all members of the Council for the Protection of Constitutional Order participated or were included, but definitely the three who were -- who were there: The president; I don't know, perhaps somebody else from the inner membership or the inner presidency. I don't know really how things proceeded from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's okay. And I won't press you about that. But after the events in Grabovica became known, the government at the highest levels took an interest in dealing with the problems in the 9th Brigade and as part of that took an interest in dealing with the guilt, if it could be established, of the killers at Grabovica; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The former part, yes. As for the latter part about guilt, I'm not sure if I understood the question properly. I am not sure if it's true that the government dealt with it. But people in certain position, certain senior officers, certain commanders, yes, they definitely did deal with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And just -- just as a -- as a summary of Trebevic: The operation had a broader focus than just merely the events in Grabovica, but nevertheless one of the focuses of Trebevic was to help investigate the crime at Grabovica; is that a fair comment?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But throughout this period there remained a reserve on behalf of the senior people, who you've described, in terms of communicating information to Sefer Halilovic; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I assume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Okay. Now, the -- I just have a very few, if you like, preliminary questions, and the way I'm going to proceed now is to ask you some of these preliminary questions concerning the month or two -- or the month or so before September of 1993. After that, I'll move to the September 1993 incidents, and that will take us easily to the end of the day, I would think. So just by way of background matters, let me just ask you some questions here. The -- the position in the army, as you understood it, was that when the state of Bosnia was formed, there was no army. Is that correct? There was no formal standing army?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were a number of experienced officers who had some experience in the old JNA who were prepared to assist in the formation of an army; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not that numerous really. I'm not sure which number of experienced officers you are talking about, but there certainly were some such officers around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you've really anticipated the next question I wanted to ask you, which was: The truth is most of the fighters and most of the officers were essentially inexperienced volunteers; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many of the commanders also had no real familiarity with the proper workings of the system of control and command; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the truth was that with the Republika Srpska army on the hills around Sarajevo shelling the civilians and threatening to create a very dangerous situation, there just wasn't time to send people to military school; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ramiz Delalic is an example of -- well, let me ask you the question. Ramiz Delalic was a person with no military education that you're aware of, who nevertheless came to command and command very effectively a good, strong fighting unit throughout 1993; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd object to that line of questioning. There are about four -- four questions in that. It's asking about another person altogether and whether the witness has knowledge of that or not, about what -- whether Ramiz Delalic was a good fighter or not or a good commander, had any training. I'm not sure that this is the -- the witness to ask such a question. And plus, the -- the question is complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in my view, you know, it's kind of serious questions built up step by step, and Mr. Delalic is a kind of important person in this case, so I believe that Defence counsel has the right to ask some questions about this person and we'll hear the answer of the witness, to his knowledge whether he knew some information about this person or not. You may proceed, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. I can't say -- Mr. Jasarevic. Just so that we don't have to go back in history, I'll ask the question again slightly differently. To your knowledge, was Ramiz Delalic a person with no formal military training who nevertheless came to command a good, strong fighting unit in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that Ramiz Delalic sometimes failed to understand what was required of him under the system of command and control?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His behaviour often gave rise to such assumptions or indicate that there were things he didn't understand, but I can't be specific about that other than what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say about Ramiz Delalic in your experience that in general he fulfilled his combat tasks effectively and without cowardice?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be allowed to elaborate on this. One could certainly say that Mr. Ramiz Delalic was a brave fighter. That much is certain. However, to the extent that I knew him, and I did said yesterday that I tried to approach him and give him a hand; if I may say that, I think you know what I mean. He was an unpredictable person. And I will clarify this too. Metaphorically speaking, in the morning he works well; in the afternoon, suddenly you see a different man there. That's what I mean when I say "unpredictable." He was a temperamental person, very lively, a live wire, prone to devious forms of behaviour from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And in -- in your efforts to -- to deal with him, you were -- you were fortunate enough to have a very competent security officer placed within the 9th Brigade, Tomo Juric. Is it the fact that Juric was a very experienced police officer before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Jasarevic. You have to actually answer in words because it's recording here. Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And, in fact, for completeness, Tomo Juric was the director of the policing and security during the Sarajevo Winter Olympics; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a man with a very high reputation. He had been chief of the state security in Zenica. He had held very high positions in the republican MUP. He had very serious assignments, top-level assignments, during the Winter Olympics back in 1984. He was highly qualified and competent within the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And from what you said yesterday -- I'm referring now to what we might call "the jeep incident." When you were discussing the jeep incident yesterday, you indicated that you, with the help of Tomo Juric, was able to persuade Ramiz Delalic to cooperate and to return that vehicle. And I just wanted to ask you about that. How was it that you managed to persuade him to do that? Can you recall how you did so?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea how I managed. There was something about my nature -- and I don't want to be blowing my own trumpet here. I was good at handling people, but it was mostly thanked to Mr. Juric that I managed to get through to Ramiz Delalic. But this is not really something that I can put my finger on right now. It's part of who I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's -- yes, sorry. And I didn't mean to embarrass you by that question. Really when -- in this court -- in this Tribunal, when we've looked at the military manuals, we've seen a great deal about orders and a great deal about lines of command, but we haven't seen very much about the term "persuasion" in those manuals, and yet is it the fact that persuasion ended up being one of the chief weapons that you had to use during this war because of the nature of the soldiers that you were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have used the term "persuasion" in a very conditional sense. Maybe it's not an adequate term, but as I had worked for a long time with the security service before the war - by the time the war started, I was not a young man after all - bearing in mind all the objective difficulties and everything that we've spoken about, we had the men that we had. The situation was not necessarily ideal. We had to find ways to deal with people. You had to train them. We had to take things in our stride, take things as we went along. I was myself no commander, and I did not have the obligation to -- to issue orders, so I tried to approach people in different ways, to make them useful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And I just want to go back for a minute to the -- that incident that you referred to when Amir Deljkic was in such trouble and you tried to help him. Now, yesterday you were asked some questions about that by my -- by the learned Prosecutor. I wanted to ask you here: You indicated that you sought to get Sefer Halilovic -- you tried to get Sefer Halilovic to come along and help -- or sorry, to -- to intervene in a way in that situation. Now, you also indicated that you -- you approached Sefer because at that time you knew him better than Rasim Delic and there were a number of reasons that -- that you gave. Could I ask you this question: In a formal sense, the authority did in fact lie with Rasim Delic. If you were to do it as a textbook situation, the authority lay with Rasim Delic to simply order to the wrongdoers, "Let that man go." That's correct, isn't it? Correct but possibly a little unrealistic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that situation, your assessment was that persuasion was needed rather than an order, because the order was likely to be completely ineffective; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with the jeep incident, in the military school in Belgrade, if they were teaching how to deal with the jeep incident, they'd probably say, "Issue an order to that villain to hand back the jeep," but -- well, that would be the textbook way to deal with it, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But really -- well, perhaps I'll -- I'll put this question another way: Those of you who had JNA experience and were able to contribute something to the proper organisation of the army were always trying to impose order, discipline, and coherence on the Bosnian army in order to make it a more effective fighting force to save Bosnia; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely. In order to organise an army, you need discipline. No discipline, no army. It can lead to all sorts of things, but not to an organised army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that in September of 1993, the -- the control and command system within the army was -- is best described in this way: Immature and incomplete and a work in progress? Now, those are my terms, not yours. But I just ask for your comment. Do you agree that that's -- those are accurate terms?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not agree fully with this. In my opinion, one can't say that throughout this period this situation prevailed across the board in the army, in terms of poor discipline, poor organisation, and poor training. It didn't apply to the army as a whole. I do believe, however, that this was indeed the case with the units we mentioned, violations of discipline I mean. Even outside the 1st Corps there were units where there was talk of indiscipline or insubordination, but these examples were not as glaring as this one. It's true that we took things in our stride, that this was a work in progress, in a manner of speaking, and we had to set up our own institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you this -- this question: In terms of behaviour such as you've indicated that's inconsistent with the proper command and control system, were all of the other brigades in Sarajevo, apart from the 9th and 10th, completely perfect, or did some of them have occasional and partial lapses and problems of the same sort as the 9th and 10th but not to the same extent as the 9th and 10th?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were definitely errors committed by other units, too, as well as lapses. Here's an example: All the units had a problem digging trenches. This was a problem with all the units, all the soldiers, or most at any rate. Most units and soldiers were unhappy whenever they came back from the front line, from combat, whenever they returned into town to see their family, to get a change of clothes, to wash. Invariably they would see young people around who could as well have been helping out on the front line. They felt that this was unfair. There were certain reactions. We never identified these people, but there were some such individuals. Digging trenches along the front line would be done in an organised way. The civil protection people would usually help, or simply citizens who lived near the front line. That was how things were normally done. But these problems were present to a much higher extent with the units that you have referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. And there's just a couple -- sorry. Yes, thank you for dealing with those matters. And there's another preliminary matter that I wanted to deal with, and this concerns -- perhaps -- actually, before I leave that matter, there's a couple of documents I'd seek to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to show the witness an order. It's Defence document D75. I'll just provide the -- the DD number. The 65 ter number is D75, and the document number is DD00.0289, and it's to be marked for exhibit -- MFI219 -- MFI -- sorry -- yes, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. I Mr. -- Mr. Jasarevic. This is a document which is -- an order and it will be brought up on the screen from front of you in a moment. I would ask you to inspect it. While it's being brought up, can I ask you that throughout the cross-examination, you're likely to be shown quite a large number of documents by me. And at any time when you have a query about the document or that it's being shown to you in the wrong way, please feel free to make that clear because otherwise I will waste your time asking you question about that. Now, do you have that -- I'm sorry. We'll just have to wait for the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could indicate this: I can ask some other questions -- some general questions while that document is being sought for and then perhaps -- perhaps come back and look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's an order concerning trench-digging that I'm going to show you, but we'll come back to it when the document is ready to be shown. And the general questions I wanted to ask concern something else now, and this is the topic of war crimes and the Bosnian state generally. Now, to your knowledge, the Republika Srpska was pursuing a policy of, putting it in the nicest way possible for them, Serbians living in a Serbian state. Is that the way you understood the position?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't really difficult to understand it in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you understood the position of the -- the more enthusiastic wing of the HVO, their position was that Croats should be entitled to live in a Croat state, so far as you understood the position; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately. We saw this as a form of betrayal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the policy of Bosnia was quite different to that. The policy of Bosnia was to promote a multi-ethnic Bosnian state; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
