utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also the fact that the Presidency of Bosnia at all times had persons from other ethnic and religious backgrounds, such as Stjepan Kljuic, or Mirko Pejanovic, Croat and Serb respectively, on the Presidency? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you'll just have to answer because of the transcript here. I'm sorry, Mr. Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And likewise the -- the very army itself, the Bosnian army, had a policy of preserving at least one Croat and one Serbian deputy commander, Stjepan Siber and Jovan Divjak respectively; is that the fact?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it the fact therefore that atrocities committed against a particular ethnic group, if committed by the Bosnian army, were in themselves an absolute disaster for the viability of the Bosnian state and the integrity of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is not only a crime. It is not only that everyone understands this to be a crime. It was seen as a fatal political blow to the very goal of our struggle, the goal that we struggled for under extremely difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as well as the individual sadness and tragedy of the killings of Croatian and, quite frankly, friendly Croatian civilians at Grabovica, that crime was a potential disaster for the goal of a multi-ethnic Bosnia because it could clearly be used to discredit that goal; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed, to your knowledge, in later times the crimes at Grabovica and Uzdol were used to that very purpose, to point out that the Bosnian army is a racial, prejudiced, Muslim force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- this line of questioning: First of all, the relevance I question. And secondly, this is a witness whose own opinion is being elicited on these rather large issues as to the goal of the army, the multi-ethnicity of the state. I'm not sure whether this witness is qualified to -- to answer such questions, Your Honour, and I still don't see the relevance either, so my objection would be on these two grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this witness is a member of the -- the BiH army and he was present at that time. He has his opinions towards certain matters. So in this aspect, I believe that this line of questioning is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But as for the last question, I'm not quite sure because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's after the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I concede --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please put your question in another way to be more specific

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I -- I think my learned friend's -- well, I agree with what Your Honour says, and I'll -- I will put that more specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, I put that question very generally. But during the time -- even -- even in the week or so after the Uzdol crime, you became aware that that was being used, if you like, in the public relations war between Croatia and Bosnia; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. What I heard was very unambiguous and that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And these goals and opinions that I've just asked you about were goals and opinions that you discussed with the senior soldiers that you dealt with, including Sefer Halilovic, during your time as a -- during your work duties in 1993; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I understood properly which goals you are thinking of. I didn't understand that part, so could you please say that again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, I should have specified that. The -- the policy of the army to discourage war crimes and to encourage a good attitude to the diverse population of Bosnia, that policy is something that you shared with Sefer Halilovic and other senior leaders of the Bosnian army and which you discussed with them from time to time and, I suggest, quite frequently in 1993. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am convinced that is so, but I wasn't any kind of authority which would chair such meetings or conversations, but all of us who used to meet shared that kind of thinking and that approach in general, including Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just excuse me one moment. Now I believe the document is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you a document marked tat top right with the -- with the letters "D75"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we have a Court number at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's DD00-- sorry, it's already assigned MFI219.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have in front of you an order by Sefer Halilovic dated the 3rd of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- and to your knowledge, on the 3rd of June, 1993 Sefer was still the number-one man in the army, although within five days he was to be replaced by Rasim Delic. Is that your understanding of his position at the time of this order?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time, he was the number-one man. There's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you notice that here a -- what is described as "a mixed commission" is established by this order to -- to deal with certain problems that are set out in paragraph 2? Perhaps I -- before I ask you that question, I should ask you a formal question myself, since I myself made objections about it. Do you recall this document yourself, this order being issued to deal with this sort of behaviour by Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't remember this document, but I'm aware of a kind of general approach in terms of this, so it's possible that I formed such a conviction which I termed "general approach" stemmed from documents similar to this one. Of course, you need to keep in mind that at the time I was not the number-one security person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. And just on that point - because I don't know that it was made clear to Their Honours when that occurred - did you -- did you take up your position as head of the SVB on or about the 18th of July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late July for sure. I'm not sure about the exact date. I think it was the 17th of July, as far as I can recall, but I can't be quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in late July for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. And -- all right. Well, that was just to clarify something. And you replaced Fikret Muslimovic at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, as you don't have a direct recollection of that document there, I'll -- I'll just ask you: Your recollection is that the commander of the army had a policy that trench-digging should be done by the proper authorities; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, because the logic was that we are taking soldiers from the trenches who need to come back to fight. We would be exhausting them, while there were others who would be available and could be used to dig trenches in order to save the strength of the soldiers and to prevent them from doing two jobs. So the answer boils down to yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, earlier on I made a reference to "textbook answers," to problems, and in this court we've heard - and I expect we'll hear again - references to the crimes involved in taking citizens to dig trenches. Now, I want to ask you a question, and you can perhaps explain to the Court, what was the need for trenches at all in Sarajevo at that time? Why were they important?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think probably the Defence counsel used the term "the crimes involved in taking citizens to dig trenches." We did not consider digging trenches a crime. We considered it to be undisciplined conduct but not a crime. So the nature of those two things is not the same. It was absolutely essential to dig trenches. In all military rules and regulations, it's important to do them and the function of doing that is clear, that is, to protect human lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if it wasn't for the digging of trenches, what -- if there were no trenches dug, would that have increased the likelihood that the Army of the Republika Srpska would have successfully occupied the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you'd all seen on television what happened to Vukovar when that was occupied by Serbian force, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the previous question was purely speculative, whether the Serb army would have gone into Sarajevo, and it continues, I think, on the next one on a more speculative note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We know that digging trenches is important for the Defence of Sarajevo, so there's no need to elaborate on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I shall move on, Your Honour. Thank you. Just -- just excuse me one moment, Mr. Jasarevic. I just have a point of law to raise here. Your Honour, in terms of the document, I offer that now as an exhibit. It may need to be argued out later on. It's not a document this witness acknowledged as seeing, but it's an official order and issued by Halilovic in his capacity at the time as -- as Chief -- he was Chief of Staff of the army. But at that time the evidence is that that was the number-one position and that on the 8th -- I think the very first or second exhibit that was tendered indicated that Rasim Delic on the 8th of June was appointed as commander of the army. So I'll indicate that I've got a basis for tendering it that I'll elaborate on later on. I don't want to waste the witness's time now. But I'll just indicate I would seek that -- offer that for tender and we'll deal with it. I want to show the witness two similar documents now just to see whether or not he has seen these ones, and if they -- he has, I'll add them to the list. Could the witness please be shown 357. The DD number is DD00.0216. And it's to be Marked for Exhibit 220.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we'll deal with the admission of the documents at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Together with the Prosecution's documents. I believe that the Prosecution also have some documents to tender. So we'll deal with them all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, with respect, I agree with that. I just wanted to show the witness the document now and see if he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: He may remember; he may not. It may be, Your Honour, because the Prosecutor has got a few documents and we've got a lot, that this could be dealt with in writing briefly rather than delay witnesses. I'm open to guidance here. But we'd be prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll see -- we'll see at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Jasarevic, I'm sorry about that delay. Do you now have in front of you D57 -- sorry, do you now -- do you now have in front of you a document dated the 26th of February, 1993, which is a -- an order from Sefer Halilovic to the command -- commands of all corps in order to eliminate the irregularities that have been observed with regard to engaging work obligation units and their proper use for work and tasks under Article 18 on work obligations? Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Would you mind just looking over that document and seeing whether -- and then telling me whether you recall seeing that document in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document before. This is a document from February 1993. Judging by the contents and the tasks, these documents usually did not come to me but it was of help to me here. I recalled this term "work units" or "work platoons." Earlier I mentioned the civilian protection, but these work units were intended to work in an organised manner on trench-digging so that the fighters who were on the lines would not be used for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Well, look, since you didn't see that document, I won't ask you questions directly about the document but just dealing with your specific memory now rather than the document, is it the case that you remember there being such work platoons and do you also remember that Sefer Halilovic had the policy of trying to regulate them in an orderly and sensible way?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can respond positively to that question. Yes, that was the general intention and something that Mr. Halilovic insisted on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks. Just generally speaking, and not -- not limited to the trenches -- the trench-digging issue, but in the year when Sefer Halilovic was the leading person in the army, did he introduce a number of sets of regulations designed to bring some sort of control and command order into the army.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he introduce the Rule on Military Courts?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that during his term of office such documents were adopted, just like the Rules on Discipline, on Military Courts, the Rules of Service for the military security service and the military police. Actually, it's quite a large number of regulations guiding the tasks and the work of the army in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they were all adopted or drafted during the term of office of Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your -- the rules governing -- governing your organisation, the SVB, were introduced, is it correct, on the 11th or 12th of September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 11th of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when Namik Dzankovic went down to Herzegovina with the inspection team, those rules had been in place for just under a year; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's maths. It's clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's -- you have me there, Mr. Jasarevic. The fact is that you -- you would -- you yourself personally and other experienced SVB officers would try to educate the volunteer soldiers and the volunteer officers in the command-and-control system whenever you had the chance to do so. I'm thinking of the jeep incident as one incident. But as a general proposition, is that true as well?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps this example with the jeep is not a good one if we're talking about training. Excuse me for saying this, but from day one there were attempts to train those people. I think that I mentioned a day or two before here that I personally, I myself, because of the circumstances - it wasn't any particular privilege of mine - organised training, for example, with senior officers of the military police in the Belgrad Hotel [phoen]. This was perhaps in August or early September of 1992. The purpose was to explain to those people what military police was. They all wanted to be military police officers but they didn't know what it was exactly. So then we published certain manuals. For example, when I was at the head of the security service, we published a manual and I mentioned that the training was conducted via the MUP and that it was completed at a higher level, at the military school in Zenica. So this points to an ongoing process of training people on the job according to the objective conditions that were prevailing and the options that were available to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just -- just so that I manage that -- the topics I want to cover; can I ask when a break is envisaged by Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you've finished a section, we could have the break right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I have finished the section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll take a break, and we'll resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we are having the witness, there's a matter I would like to announce, that is, tomorrow, March 3rd, we'll hold a hearing which will take place in room 177 in this Tribunal at 11.30. The first part of this hearing will be ex parte, which is mainly dealing with the motions filed by the Defence team. The reason for that, first, I believe that those motions has to be dealt with as soon as possible; secondly, we have a very tight schedule. I have to say that we are a little bit behind our trial schedule, so we could not eat the Prosecution's time any more. Thirdly, recently there are a lot of activities in this Tribunal: For instance, the trials -- six trials going on simultaneously, and there are a lot of Initial Appearances, so we could not possibly find a courtroom. So we'll arrange it in room 177, and the Defence team will be gathered in the lobby and my legal assistants will show them into that location. The second part of this hearing, we will require the presence of the Prosecution. This part of the hearing will concern the Defence request to be allowed access to the criminal records of ten witnesses for the Prosecution who are to appear or have already appeared before this Tribunal. The urgent motion for immediate disclose filed on the 16th December 2004 and the following submissions by both parties regarding in general the Prosecution's witnesses as suspects will also be discussed. The second part of hearing will commence at 12.30. In order to provide the Prosecution with the opportunity to prepare for this hearing, the Trial Chamber will lift the ex parte status of the following Defence filings: First, addendum to further Defence report re access to further material. This addendum was filed on 24th November, 2004. Secondly, additional motion re criminal record of Prosecution witnesses filed on the 5th January 2005, with the exception of paragraph 22. Thirdly, additional motion re criminal records of Prosecution's witnesses filed on the 11th February 2005. These filings will remain confidential. And by the way, there's no need for the parties to wear their robes for this hearing. That's all for the announcement. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, those matters are matters that will be conducted by my co-counsel in the matter, Mr. Mettraux, because of preparing for other matters, I would prefer to be excused. But if the Chamber wishes me to be present, I will. But Mr. Mettraux will be handling the argument in respect of those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand that, you know, we have limited space in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm going to say that each party should at most -- for three people to take part in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we can subtract 16 and a half stone from the Defence contribution by my absence, and I'm grateful for the indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. Mr. Jasarevic, that completes my questions about the -- the preliminary sort of matters, and I now move to the -- the matters in September of 1993. Now, first of all, I just have some questions arising out of the appointment of -- of Namik Dzankovic to the position of security -- or SVB representative subordinated to Sefer Halilovic on the inspection team. Now, you indicated yesterday what you understood to be the training and the background of Mr. Dzankovic. I want to be clear that I understood you correctly. Dzankovic was certainly not present when his name was assigned to this inspection team; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, I think from what you indicated earlier he was already in the zone of responsibility of the 6th Corps or possibly the 4th Corps at the time when he was selected and indeed part of the reason for selecting him was that he was already in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that -- that there were certain, if you like, shortcomings -- well, I withdraw that question. I'll put it another way. Mr. Dzankovic may not have been the most highly trained individual ever to belong to the SVB, but he was an intelligent, educated, and so far as you could see, very honest person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to clarify this, Your Honours. I said this and this is a fact: Mr. Dzankovic is a highly educated person. I believe he holds a degree in economics. Naturally he had not been trained as an officer or as a security officer before the war. As a result of these circumstances that I spoke about, he ended up with the security administration. He was an honourable person. He did have some experience. This was in the second half of 1993. It wasn't really so much his experience as a security officer, but he had taken part in interviews in what we call "operative work." He did have some experience, but you certainly couldn't call him a trained security officer, not to a degree that would have been desirable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Somewhere there is a reference to his having been on Igman at a previous time, and I just wonder if -- if you're able to comment about that, whether he'd had any function on Igman either in July or in August before he set off for Herzegovina. Do you recall anything to that effect? And if so, are you able to tell us what his role was there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, very well. Well, at -- I'm not attempting to represent Mr. Dzankovic as being an Olympic champion, but had he have been an obvious disaster, you would not have selected him to perform the function which he was assigned. Is that a fair comment to make?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly he wouldn't have made it to the security administration. There can be no talk of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. And I suppose my final question about that is that when he was assigned to this inspection team, that was done obviously with the knowledge of Sefer Halilovic; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not something that I can answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you're certainly not aware of any pre-existing relationship between Halilovic and Namik Dzankovic; am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that Sefer actually knew Dzankovic. Probably he knew Dzankovic by virtue of Dzankovic's position, but I can't even claim that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. I'm sorry -- I'm sorry, Mr. Jasarevic. A potential translation ambiguity has arisen there. Did you say to us just then that Sefer knew Dzankovic by virtue of Dzankovic's position or did you mean that Dzankovic knew Sefer because of Sefer's position?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other way around. Sefer held an important position. He was known to fighters from across the country. They saw him in the media. Sefer would not necessarily have known even all the brigade commanders, let alone an operations officer. That would have been a practical impossibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, I want to turn to the issue that was raised by the Prosecutor concerning the SVB's role in some circumstances in making a security assessment. Now, the question is going to be posed in a general way, but I'll soon relate it to the specific case in Grabovica. So first of all, in the event that a force of approximately, say, 200 to 300 soldiers was to be billeted -- was to be taken from Sarajevo and billeted far away in Herzegovina, would you expect local units with local knowledge to play some part in the security assessment that had to be made in respect of those travelling troops?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is quite a complex question. That is how I see it. May I therefore be allowed to elaborate? First of all, I don't think I would myself refer to specific figures, hundreds of people. I'd prefer to use a unit, battalion, company, brigade, because that might help us understand what follows. In every army, you have something called a march. A battalion-level unit or a brigade-level unit, for example, is being transferred from one place to another. This transfer, the act itself, is called "a march." They may walk or they may drive, but it's called "a march." Prior to that, assessments are carried out. If possible, the military police are normally used or reconnaissance units to help these units along. It is, however, important to say that these transfers or marches or whatever you call it, the act of taking a unit from one place to another, are clearly envisaged and regulated by orders, orders on how to organise combat activity, orders on how to organise a march, because that is the military term. That is how these activities are organised. I'm not sure if I should go on about local units. You referred to local units. You probably mean the receiving unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I indicate that -- that you are permitted to go on, but I'll -- I'll clarify a couple of matters so that -- so that you can do so. Yes, I am referring specifically to the receiving units. And when I come to the concrete example that I will come to so that there's no trickery here for you. The concrete example I will come to is the unit which in this case we know was the receiving unit, and that unit was the unit of Zulfikar Alispago, which was based in Jablanica or Donja Jablanica, but which had responsibility or at least had control over, in some respects, the village of Grabovica. So that's the direction in which my questions are going, and you feel free to continue as you were.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand that to be a trick question. I just wanted to be sure that I understood the question. So as I have pointed out, Your Honours, in cases like these, there needs to be an order, a marching order or an order to designate an area that the is being sent to. I do not know of any such order, as I have said countless times, nor did I know at the time which units were in the area, whether it was Zulfikar Alispago's unit, a unit of the 4th or 6th Corps. I didn't know where the units were going or why. I'm not sure if I'm able to answer the question in a valid way. At any rate, when a unit arrives in an area, it can't just be left to its own devices having reached a particular village with no military preparations, with no logistics, with no security support involving units of the military police. They must check the area beforehand. In this particular case, you need to bear in mind that the village of Grabovica had found itself in the middle of combat activity before. HVO members were involved in hand-to-hand combat in the area or just outside the area. They remained just outside the area, which was a danger to any unit coming in. The ground had not been prepared, in a manner of speaking, and this was always a potential danger for the incoming units. There might be an ambush. The ground might be mined. What we refer to as "camps" or the units' deployment in the waiting areas is something that would have required an organisational order, as I said yesterday, and particularly an assessment with a detailed description of how the assignment was to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And -- well, I understand those points that you make. And I want to ask you: What -- I don't want to ask you about facts that are outside of your knowledge, but I want to ask you to comment on certain matters, and you comment on them as best you can, but also tell us whether it's within your knowledge specifically or whether it's just a comment from theory, if that's okay. But the matters I'm going to put to you are this: Did you know is that as a matter of fact it was -- or did you at the time know when it happened that it was indeed Zulfikar's unit that had the responsibility to receive and to -- to billet or accommodate the units that came down from Sarajevo? Was that within your knowledge at the time when it happened?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Even so, because of your knowledge of the SVB system, I would still want to persist and ask you some questions about what should happen. The -- what were the obligations as you understand it of the Zulfikar unit and, in particular, its security representative upon learning that it was their task to receive and accommodate the units that were coming from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that. The witness has very clearly said he does not know, and now we are being asked what the -- what the particular job was of the particular unit, which the witness has clearly stated he does not know. So I'd object on that ground, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may be able to deal with the matter another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- yes. Yes, there should be some basis, you know, to ask this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- particular witness about that particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, I agree with that. But it may be that he can comment on certain particulars of the evidence because of his high level of expertise, which the Prosecutor referred to yesterday -- or on the first day of his examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look, I'll ask some factual questions first. I'm sorry, Mr. Jasarevic. Did you know the name of -- of the security SVB officer who was attached to Zulfikar Alispago's unit at Donja Jablanica in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's -- I just can't recall now where, but does -- it doesn't matter where. Was there -- does the name Smail Hodzic, S-m-a-i-l H-o-d-z-i-c ring any bells at all in your mind in terms of that matter?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it incumbent upon -- and I appreciate you don't know the name of -- of Zulfikar Alispago's security man -- was it necessary for that person to contact you personally over details such as the accommodation of soldiers from Sarajevo? Is that something you would expect to have heard about or was it too much of a local issue for him to trouble you about?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. There was no need and he was physically not in a position to do that. He couldn't have reached me. The distance was too great. And in a formal sense, this unit was within the establishment of the 6th Corps until the 1st of September. And from then on, as far as I remember, it was part of the 4th Corps. These are many steps to be taken before he could eventually reach me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in terms of the -- his ability to contact you, are you able to explain what is the precise mechanism by which that person would contact you, if he had to do so? For example, was there a local telephone network? Was there a computer packet system? Would you mind just explaining to the Tribunal so that they understand what the -- what the distance between Sarajevo and Jablanica really meant, in terms of communications.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an enormous difficulty and an objective one. The enemy forces split the two areas in half. The communications system was a source of problems. There were technical problems and there were security-related problems too. The system needed protecting and all the messages were coded. It usually took some time to decode the messages. This was a real problem. I don't think what it -- what it would have taken for a security officer attached to a company-strong unit to get in touch with the security chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, that was going to be my next question, but yes, you've answered it. Thanks. So look, can I just put a couple of propositions to you. I'll bear in mind my learned friend's objections too, but I just want to put to you a couple of propositions about this. First of all, you don't know yourself what Zulfikar's security officer did with respect to receiving the Sarajevo troops; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, according to standard procedures, that person should have performed a security assessment relating to those troops, including a consideration of where they were to be billeted; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you could say that about the area that the unit was coming to, but as for the unit itself, it needed to be assessed by its own brigade, its own brigade which originally sent the unit out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that respect, with -- with respect to the 9th Brigade, that would mean Tomo Juric, the security officer there? Can you say who should have performed that assessment with respect to the 2nd Independent Battalion, which the evidence is was also sent? First of all, I should ask you: Do you know the 2nd Independent Battalion under the command of Adnan Solakovic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes., I know about the battalion. It was based in Sarajevo. But I didn't realise that they were off at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Well -- well, that's okay. The evidence is that they were there. But my question to you doesn't require you to speculate about that. It is that if the 2nd Independent Battalion was sent out from Sarajevo, who should have performed a security assessment concerning them? Did they have their own security person, or should it have been the corps level? Would you just explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an independent battalion, and according to some military principles, it has the rank of a brigade. When it's independent, it has its own security officer, and the security situation was evaluated by that person. There was no need for the corps to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I see. So that the -- effectively the 2nd Independent Battalion ought to have performed -- am I right in summarising this way, that they should have performed their own security assessment? Is that right, or am I getting it completely wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. A local unit -- well, look, I withdraw that. But in any event, the persons performing that function, that security assessment function, were not under any obligation, nor was it necessary for them to report directly to you about these activities; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that level, the units were not obliged to submit reports to me. They had their own superiors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Okay. Well, I understand that. Just finally -- I appreciate you've given indications that you don't know a great deal about the situation with Zulfikar's unit, so I won't ask you any more questions about that, except for this one only: Were you aware that before the -- before this Operation Neretva 93 at one stage Zulfikar Alispago and at least some of his units were on Igman -- involved in the combat on Igman? Was that within your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'm aware that that unit was at Igman and that it took part in fighting in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the proposition I'm coming to -- the question I'm going to ask you in the end really, I suppose, apart from all these preliminary ones, is this: To your knowledge, Zulfikar Alispago was personally acquainted with Ramiz Delalic and had met him, both on Igman and in other situations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The witness has been asked to comment whether two people met on Igman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's exactly what I am asking him, yes. And it seems to be a relevant and admissible question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was -- the witness didn't say he was at Igman. He said he knew there was an operation, and the -- Zulfikar Alispago was there. Perhaps he should be asked whether he was there to know whether they met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the question is to the witness's knowledge, just to say, you know, whether he knows or not. Maybe he was not there but he knew about that. Well, we'll see, you know, how the witness will answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Jasarevic, the water was muddied by me asking a preliminary question when I really just need to come to the straight-ahead question now, and that is: To your knowledge, did Zulfikar Alispago know Ramiz Delalic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Thank you. Well, those are the preliminary questions. And I now want to come to some questions about the -- about the incidents in Grabovica and, in particular, your knowledge about those and -- and what you can -- and perhaps what you can explain about some of the documents that we have to deal with here. I want to preface these questions to you by mentioning this: I'm going to show you a large number of documents and some of which have been found in archives, some of which you may have seen, some of which you may not. And if at any time you feel the need to stop and read a document or to be assured of where it comes from, you're perfectly entitled to do that. This is not an exercise in trickery, and you're entitled to knowledge about the documents. So bear that in mind if a document comes that you may not have seen and, as I say, feel free to interrupt or to ask -- or to raise any issue that you want to in the course of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, just excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness be given the opportunity, please, to look at -- it's Defence document, 65 ter D66. Its DD number is DD00.0255, and it will become MFI221. Your Honours, I just want to note something for the Court's benefit here, that this document was shown -- an identical document was shown to the witness yesterday. It's -- it's the Dzankovic report. But the translation that we are showing is -- we think it's a more full translation because there -- I think there was a stamp on it, which is not translated, and we just weren't sure with the situation yesterday when -- you probably don't recall, but there was a lot of shuffling at this table when that document was displayed. And we should indicate that now in case the Prosecution wonders why we're using an identical document and giving it a different number. This one has got a slightly different translation, only as to a stamp, and indeed that may not be a matter of massive significance. But I mention it now so that everyone knows what's coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there might be some significance to the other party. I wonder whether the Prosecution has been properly informed about the differences of the two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, yes or no,

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have not been informed of anything. It would be something that counsel could have perhaps indicated to us ahead of time and we could actually have looked and found the document. I can see our case manager is now looking through to find them. Your Honour, this is a part of the function of not having Defence documents prior to their cross-examination. This is a matter I had raised with you some time ago, that at least a day ahead of time that the Defence be required to also give us their list, like we give them our list - and a very detailed list, Your Honour - and assist us in preparing so that the proceedings go along in a more expeditious manner and this kind of time-wasting doesn't happen, because we would like to verify whether that is indeed -- there's any issues in translations and things, and of course it will take some time to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we -- we have got the Defence list the day before yesterday. I don't know whether you have got it on that day or not. Mr. Morrissey, do you have the signature of the Prosecution for receiving that list of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'll have to check that with someone who knows the answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Do you mind to show that document with the stamps and the different translation to the Prosecution right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's -- Your Honour, it's uploaded. It should be on the screen or capable of being on the screen. It's -- Your Honour, this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, this was the document that appeared on the ELMO yesterday. I think it's -- I think there's a misunderstanding here. There was some communication between the Defence and the Prosecution about this. I am now at the moment in the middle of asking questions of a witness on a key document and I don't want to be sidetracked. Let me say that I'll use the Prosecution document now so that there's no argument about it. I do not want my friend's criticism to stand, but I'll deal with it later. There's a witness here who needs to give evidence. So I'll use the Prosecutor's document, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's MFI215. And we'll point out what the problems are with the Prosecutor's one at a later stage and we'll give them the opportunity to withdraw their comments if they need to withdraw them. Very well. Could the witness please be shown that, MFI215, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, there's one matter. I've just seen the transcript, where Your Honour asked the Defence counsel whether we have got the list of the documents, which you yourself have indicated you got a day before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: We don't have it. We've never been given a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean the -- the --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The Defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The documents intended to be used by Defence counsel in the cross-examination of this witness? You don't have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have never been provided it. And this is a matter that I had raised. At least we should have it a day before. If they can provide it to Your Honours, I'd imagine it would be quite simple to provide it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm surprised to hear that, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, let me indicate: As I understood the position, the Prosecutor has tried three times to get us to do this, and Your Honour has ruled against them. Now, if we need to go and find the transcript of that, we will. In cross-examination we do not have to provide them in advance with a list of the documents we're going to put to the witness. It's not the practice here; it's never been. And we would resist strongly any requirement that we do. And, Your Honour, if -- I don't want this one to be resolved on the run now. If my friend is making a serious submission, she should indicate why it is that Your Honours' ruling of the past was wrong and we should deal with it not in an ad hoc way. Because this -- well, I don't want to make a speech about it. Your Honour, not only does the Defence not have to provide it to the -- to the Prosecutor, but the Prosecutor tried to get this before and Your Honour ruled against them. We give it to the Court but we're not required to give it to the Prosecutor, and frankly, we're not going to unless there's an order that we have to, and at the moment we've got an order from Your Honour that we don't have to. If there's an interest of justice, the Prosecutors can seek to litigate it in the future. As to this particular document here, it's my opinion and it will be my submission when I've got time to deal with it that in effect we are right and they're wrong. However, for the purposes of this witness being here and giving evidence in a case that -- Your Honour, I'm acutely aware that at all times Mr. Halilovic is in custody, so I do wish to press on with the -- with the case. The Prosecutor objects, so I won't use that document now. Could I ask that if the Prosecutor wish to persist with this application of theirs, it be done formally and we do it at an appropriate time when we're not in the middle of -- of cross-examining. Because we do have a ruling which my friend has just at the moment forgotten about from Your Honour on this very topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course we made a ruling on that issue already, and the -- at the same time, we also said that it will be greatly facilitating the proceedings if the Defence counsel in their cross-examination is kind enough to provide a preliminary list to the Court as well as to the other parties before you are starting the cross-examination. It's not obligatory request, but I think in the courtesy to the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Here, you know, we met with some problem, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- there are two things to say in response to what Your Honour says. There may be occasions when it's appropriate for the Defence to do that, and I bear in mind what Your Honour says about a courtesy to the -- to the Prosecution. There's a necessity to disclose it to the Court because of the e-court situation. We have to do that. And because of the e-court situation, we're very happy to -- that the Court -- that the Judges as well as the officials in the court have that -- have those materials. But it's also the case that many documents are uploaded which may not ultimately be used in cross-examination because, as is apparent with this witness and other witnesses, sometimes a witness will answer a question without regard to a particular document and then there's no need to clutter the system proving what is testified in an uncontradicted way. And -- and for those reasons, it -- it's the fact that what is provided to the court deputies here may not represent what's put. In fact, they will have more documents than what we end up putting because some documents are there, one might say, to -- to meet contingencies. If a witness gives a particular answer, they might want to be shown a document to deal with that answer. And that's why it is that we would not be -- that's one of the reasons why the Prosecutor ought not to be given the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But -- but the situation here is a little bit different because we have two same documents with the different translation or with a stamp in one document. I think, you know, you have to inform the other party about that difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just say one thing: I agree with that. Could I just take one moment to take instructions. Because I think there's an answer to my friend's objection, and if it's the one I think it is, I'm going to make a grouchy submission. But would Your Honour just allow me to take instructions from Mr. Cengic for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I am going to make a grouchy reply. Your Honour, what happened here was that the Prosecution's original exhibit had an English translation and a Bosnian original. The Bosnian original was lacking certain markings. The Prosecution then sought the Defence's permission to use the Defence's Bosnian original. And that's what happened. Now what we want to do is to use the Defence's translation. That translation reflecting the Bosnian version that we gave to the Prosecutor that was the better version, which they used, and as to which now they seem to be suggesting that there's some dirty trick being played or that they've been disadvantaged, when in fact what is being put is the translation of the document we gave them in the spirit of cooperation and which, as I understand it, was used on the ELMO. We apologise for the inconvenience that we have caused the Prosecutor. We undertake to rectify the inconvenience that we've caused the Prosecutor. We regret, however, the way in which this was used in what seems to have been -- well, it doesn't matter about that. I withdraw that. To the extent that we've caused difficulty, we apologise for it. We will make it right. We'll provide a copy of that correct translation to the Prosecutor to follow the correct original that we gave to the Prosecutor. And then they'll have the benefit of both of the Defence documents and they won't be disadvantaged or deprived of equality of arms any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, just one question, if you don't mind: That is, who did the translation of that document? Is it by the CLSS or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm instructed it was by CLSS. You mean our translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, your translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. It's by CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And how about the Prosecution's translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I believe the Prosecution -- I don't know. They can tell you that. But I assume the CLSS probably translated their one, referring to an original which lacked the markings, which have caused all the interest in the first place. That's what I think is the situation. Your Honour, perhaps it can be clarified -- Your Honour, the truth of the matter is we should have given the additional document. We should have given it over. I mean, the reason why we didn't is because the way it happened and because we gave them the original ourselves in the first place. That's how it's come about, Your Honour. But even so we -- I don't want to cause trouble over it. Yes, we gave them the original. Yes, we should also have given them a translation of that. We didn't think of it, and you can see why we didn't, because of the -- what's unfolded here. Your Honours perhaps rather than thinking on my feet about this at the end of the day, in which -- I mean, I'm not sure how entertaining I'm being to Mr. Jasarevic here frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this moment, I think I have to make a ruling. As for this particular document, the Defence has to furnish that document with a proper translation to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we undertake to do so. It's -- it is uploaded in the system now. It's released. I think they have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And as for the admission of those documents, we'll discuss it at a later stage, especially maybe sometime without the witness present, because it's purely a translation issue or the administrative issue, which has nothing to do with this witness. So -- yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, be that as it may - and we don't have to do it now - I would invite Your Honours to reconsider your decision about the Defence documents not to be given to us in time. It is not Tribunal practice that they're not given. In fact, I can name four cases immediately - Strugar, Brdjanin/Talic, Bosanski Samac, Tuta/Stela - where this has been done. And it's done for precisely this reason. So it is not that it's not Tribunal practice. And as I said, the Prosecution would invite Your Honours because normally we've been getting documents without translation, and it does put us in a situation where we -- we are embarrassed by not having the documents in time. So as I said, we do not have to do it now, but I would certainly put it on the cards that we would invite Your Honours to -- to reconsider this aspect, and perhaps Your Honours can also look into the other cases as to how this was done and why it was done. And now with the e-court I think it's even more compelling that -- that this ought to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about the other cases at this moment, but I have to remind you that I was the Presiding Judge in Tuta and Stela's case. I know that case, you know, pretty well. I believe our court deputy was also sitting in that case. But anyway, we'll do some research on that issue and we'll continue the proceedings with this witness. I see -- yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I see everybody is nodding. So, Mr. Morrissey, would you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I'm instructed that there are a number of other cases that may be relevant, and I can list those: There's the Kunarac decision, Krnojelac, and there's the Tuta and Stela case that Your Honour mentioned. There's Blagojevic, which Your Honour was also involved in. Your Honour, could I just mention this: It's a valiant performance by my learned friend here. If my friend is serious, this ought to be done in writing in a motion. It -- Your Honours' ruled and Your Honours' rulings are no to be overturned just because the Prosecutor saw an opportunity for a brief glimpse before the matter arose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, I think I made a ruling that we'll proceed with this witness. Let's not debate on that issue at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Certainly. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd ask that the witness be shown MFI221.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I apologise to you for my part in all of that. And do you now have in front of you that document? Sorry, may I inquire, Mr. Jasarevic, do you now have in front of you a document which is dated the 13th of September, 1993 which is marked "Attention: Jusuf Jasarevic."

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "66." That's what it says in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the document. Okay. Thank you. Now, to return to -- to the case at hand here. Is this -- does this appear to be the same document that you looked at when my learned friend was cross-examining you -- or sorry, was -- was examining you in chief yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did look at this document, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now we're going to look at it slightly more thoroughly and I'm going to take you through it step by step, if that's possible. First of all, could you just indicate that the handwritten part of this document, which is addressed to Vahid, is addressed to a man called Vahid Bogunic, who was an employee of yours or an officer of yours?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the instructions there that you gave include the consulting of a legal officer, whose name you provided yesterday. And would you mind repeating that name, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Radovic [phoen], a lawyer with the security administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Now, those notes of yours were placed on this document at a later time when you finally received it; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I laid my hands on it and familiarised myself with the substance, I put the notes there. That was my usual modus operandi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, apart from it being addressed to you, is it addressed to or marked to the attention of any other person, this document, either at the start or at the end?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the answer is no. The document is addressed to the security administration generally. You can see my name in the brackets, but it could have been received by another officer who was standing in for me while I was away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. And -- well, that was my next question. Is it apparent on the face of the document who received it, yourself or another officer, or can that just not be told at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can see on the face of this is that it was received by the security administration and that's what matters, isn't it? And specifically, the reason you see my name here is probably because I was a representative of the administration, but I don't believe that is the only relevant thing about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What I want to do now is take you to some specifics in the text. Now, first of all, do you notice a reference to the relationship between the Zulfikar unit commander and the local population? It's at the start of the second large paragraph, the third paragraph altogether. Do you notice there that it says that "Bosnian army members, particularly the Zulfikar unit commander, and the Jablanica municipality civilian authorities, treated the population in a correct manner and no drastic cases of putting their security at risk were recorded"? Do you see that passage there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found the passage, but I know that it is in the document somewhere. I do acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Would you look -- just so that we can make sure that you're following what I'm putting to you, that -- the paragraph I'm referring to -- the first paragraph is -- begins "On the 8th of September, 1993 ..." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following paragraph begins with the words "The units were quartered in Croatian houses ..." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The paragraph after that commences "Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, army members, particularly the Zulfikar unit commander." I'm sorry, on the English version it's got a paragraph break, but on your version it hasn't. It's probably about seven or eight lines down from the top.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean "Zulfikar" in quotation marks?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then it goes on. The word is "civilian authorities."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. I see the passage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you also see that -- on the following line or following couple of lines, there's a reference to "The units from Sarajevo were quartered in Marica Kuce and a makeshift barrier was erected at the entrance where they controlled the entry and exit of persons"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a part of the text here that is dark and it's very unclear. I think it begins with the figures "8" or "9". Probably the year is 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I wonder whether you have the B/C/S version. Could it be furnished to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in court we don't have the B/C/S version, but we will produce it immediately, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe your friend will have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Indeed we -- we like to help the Defence, Your Honour, and we can furnish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps that document from the Prosecutor should be returned and we'll produce the document that we have. Grateful as we are for its production.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Mr. Jasarevic, just take the time and familiarise yourself with that passage. The question I'm leading to here is that -- and perhaps I can ask the question while you're -- while you're perusing it. There was a document attached to this report of Dzankovic, was there not?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm going to show you that document in a moment, but -- but just now do you recall that it was a report from the deputy head of the Jablanica police station, a man named Salih Amidzic.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ahmet Salih Amidzic. Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And generally speaking -- generally speaking, I'm not asking you to do a word-by-word comparison, because of course there are some differences, but as far as you could see, Dzankovic's report was consistent with the letter of Salih Amidzic in the details that it furnished. And this is only a broad, impressionistic question that I'm asking, but it's one which may impact on how you proceed. Was that your perception, that the two documents seemed to be broadly consistent?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm going to press on with this document now. Was information then provided by Dzankovic that over the night of the 8th and 9th of December -- sorry, of September -- that gunshots could be heard essentially lasting all night long and that in the morning a rumour came to Jablanica that -- that soldiers from Sarajevo had slaughtered the Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the text clearly reflects that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, can I indicate there's two reasons why I'm taking you to this. First of all, even though you're aware of the contents in some respects, I want some of it to appear on the transcript. And a second purpose is to -- is to clarify some of the -- of the work that was done by the services, both the SVB and by the -- by the military police. Now, the next thing -- the next paragraph reveals that "In a cooperative venture, a military policeman and a civilian policeman both went to Grabovica. Namely, those people being -- they're not named in the text here, but that was Salih Amidzic and a man called Sead Kurt [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And at that stage of the -- at that stage of proceedings, it was perfectly appropriate and acceptable for the civilian police and the -- and the military police to go cooperatively to the village to find out what they could find out; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the proviso that I'm not in the position to comment on the exact degree of their cooperation for the simple reason that their cooperation in that area did not yield the expected -- or rather, desired result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I understand your reservation about that. But I just want to get your comment about a couple of aspects of this report. The next paragraph reveals details of a -- or at least references to an interview between Salih Amidzic and two of the surviving Bosnian Croatian civilians, Ivan and Stoja Pranjic. And you'll see that in the paragraph -- in the section beginning "On the 10th of September, 1993, the Jablanica SJB chief interviewed Ivan ..." Now, do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at this point, it -- it was appropriate and -- and indeed -- sorry, I take that back. It was an appropriate thing for Dzankovic to do to report to you the steps taken by the civilian police at that time as part of his reporting up the professional line; is that accurate or -- or wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is accurate in part, but I do have to add something, Your Honours. It's a good thing that Dzankovic passed the report on to me saying that a war crime had occurred. He did his best. However, it's me who's being asked the question, and even if his report did have the properties that Defence counsel has referred to, I don't think it would have changed anything. My role was nearly useless, with the exception of instructions that I provided him with after I had received this document. There were tasks to the 1st Corps, to the analytical department concerning the reporting process. I apologise for elaborating at such length, but here the important thing was to identify the key problem, and that was organising the control over the operation, because this sort of report and this sort of information about the crime had to reach the right person on the ground, and this person would have been the only person to take appropriate steps and measures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I understand what you say about that, and I just want to elaborate, if I could, on what your -- what your possible role was. First of all, you had many duties that you had to attend to in Sarajevo, apart from assisting Dzankovic with advice and -- and -- and counsel. Is that the fact? You had a lot of things to do?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was possible that I would not have learned anything about this at the time. I was, after all, unaware of the operation itself. It was only thanks to Dzankovic's report and the phone call that I had received in the evening hours on the 11th that I found out about the crime. Had it not been for that, I probably would have found out much later, and the question remains: What good could it have been for me to find out at all at such a late stage?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I understand that. And I think I'm going to get you to explain in a moment the type of assistance that the rules require you to get to a -- a junior officer such as Dzankovic. But just now I just want to stay at the general level, and the general question is this: There was no requirement for you, nor was it a proper thing for you to do, to go down to Herzegovina and involve yourself in this case directly. Is that the fact?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. And -- but nevertheless, where a junior officer appeals to you for help and indicates the steps he wants to take or proposes to take and reports to you, then in that situation naturally you are prepared to give him such help as is appropriate in the circumstances; is that right

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He submitted a report. At the end of this report - and I'm sorry for skipping to the end of the document; perhaps I'm upsetting your strategy - but I don't think that he's precisely asking for assistance, because I don't think he was clear about his own role over there. Maybe I'm overreaching myself, but it was maybe pursuant to Mr. Halilovic's instructions that he's making these proposals. And I'm not sure who these proposals are being made to instead of trying to get the situation resolved on the ground. And we must bear in mind the fact that I received this document on the 20th of September, which means 11 or 12 days after the actual crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. And I can assure you that you're not wrecking any strategy at all. It's -- you're quite right to go forward to those -- to the end of the -- of the document, as you did, which I'm going to do in just a moment. But -- well, look, perhaps -- well, since you've done so, and lest it appear that I'm attempting to use a strategy, which I'm not, perhaps if we'd go to the end of that document now and I'll come back to some of the other minor points that I wanted to make in a moment. It's apparent to you that -- that Dzankovic was indicating what he'd been told by Sefer Halilovic not just about Halilovic's own views of the crime but about the tasks which Halilovic had -- had ordered him to perform. And all I want to do is ask you about the juxtaposition of his comments about Halilovic and then following that the proposals that Dzankovic appears to make in the document. Now, you partially anticipated this question a moment ago in your answer, but feel free to elaborate on that. It may be the last question of the night, I think, given the time. But I'd just like you to comment on those matters. You see where -- where he indicate what is Halilovic has told him to do, and then he proposes certain measures. Does it appear to you that he's proposing those measures directly as a result of the order given to him by Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me it's not explicit, but it's certainly possible. What I certainly recognise is that Mr. Halilovic gave him an assignment. This was a move that could only be welcomed. However, when commenting on this document, I clearly said that I also took into account the tasks proposed by Dzankovic. Who is he proposing this to? That is the question. Is this just a consideration on his part? Is this just something that he believes should be done? I think the real question here, Your Honours, is that these assignments are unrealistic, inappropriate. And when I say "unrealistic" I mean in terms of the resources, in terms of the unit strength, in terms of the time. And that applies to most of these assignments. That's what I mean when I say "unrealistic." And that, I think, is a great difficulty with this particular portion of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I have more questions about this, but they're not going to be finished in one minute, Your Honour, so it may be appropriate to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But we are approaching to the weekend. Could you please be kind enough to inform us how much time you still need to finish your cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I indicate that it will be shorter than I expected. I -- I intend to complete my cross-examination tomorrow with this witness. Because there's a large number of documents, it's possible that it would go into the following day, but it's also possible and it's my intention to complete it tomorrow. That's -- that's the goal. So we'll try that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The hearing for today is adjourned.
